problem_statement: Zephyr's k_timer API gives no way for external modules to observe a timer's lifecycle (initialization, start, stop, expiry) without modifying the kernel. A module needs to be able to register observers that are notified whenever a k_timer is initialized, started, stopped, or expires, and to do so without changing kernel internals. These observer hooks should fire exactly alongside the timer's own behaviour: each registered observer's on_init must be called when k_timer_init() completes, on_start when k_timer_start() starts the timer, on_stop when k_timer_stop() stops an active timer, and on_expiry in lock-step with the timer's own expiry callback.

problem_statement_fixed: Zephyr's k_timer API gives no way for external modules to observe a timer's lifecycle (initialization, start, stop, expiry) without modifying the kernel. A module needs to be able to register observers that are notified whenever a k_timer is initialized, started, stopped, or expires, and to do so without changing kernel internals. The feature is gated behind the Kconfig option CONFIG_TIMER_OBSERVER. Observers are registered at compile time using the K_TIMER_OBSERVER_DEFINE(name, init, start, stop, expiry) macro, which takes a name for the observer entry and four callback function pointers. The callback functions must have the following signatures: on_init(struct k_timer *timer), on_start(struct k_timer *timer, k_timeout_t duration, k_timeout_t period), on_stop(struct k_timer *timer), on_expiry(struct k_timer *timer). These observer hooks should fire exactly alongside the timer's own behaviour: each registered observer's on_init must be called when k_timer_init() completes, on_start when k_timer_start() starts the timer, on_stop when k_timer_stop() stops an active timer, and on_expiry in lock-step with the timer's own expiry callback.
